standard.title: Generate, communicate and compare designs
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explored problems for known users and generated simple design ideas through describing, drawing or modelling (AC9TDE2P01 — Design Technologies equivalent; AC9TDI2P01 for DT problem investigation). They have not yet worked with explicit comparison of design ideas against user stories or design criteria.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students generate multiple design ideas for a digital solution, communicate those ideas clearly, and compare them against user stories and design criteria to identify the most suitable approach.

nodes.label: Generating multiple design ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can generate more than one design idea for a given problem and describe what each idea proposes
nodes.minimum_width: Generate at least two different design ideas for a simple problem and sketch or describe each one
nodes.typical_width: Brainstorm multiple design ideas for a problem, accepting all suggestions as possibilities; describe each idea in enough detail to distinguish it from the others
wider: Generate design ideas for a problem with a First Nations Australian community context — explore how different ideas might reflect different cultural considerations or access constraints

Use a structured brainstorming technique (e.g. SCAMPER or random prompt) to generate ideas beyond obvious solutions — discuss how forced variation produces ideas that wouldn't emerge from direct thinking

response_modes.reason: Students in early design experience tend to converge on the first idea they think of. Generating ideas for varied problem contexts builds the habit of ideating before selecting — a phase-critical behaviour for the design cycle.

success_criteria: Produces at least two visibly different design ideas
Describes what each idea would do, not just what it would look like
nodes.hinge_reason: Students with only one design idea cannot meaningfully compare in N3 — comparison requires at least two distinct ideas. Convergence on a single idea makes the evaluation step trivial.

nodes.label: Communicating design ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can communicate a design idea to peers clearly enough for others to understand what it proposes
nodes.minimum_width: Sketch or describe one design idea so that a peer can understand what the solution would do
nodes.typical_width: Communicate design ideas using sketches, annotations or verbal explanation; include enough detail about what the solution does, who it is for, and how users interact with it
wider: Communicate a design idea that would work for users in an unfamiliar context (e.g. a tool for a ranger group) — discuss what extra information a person unfamiliar with the context would need to understand the design
Compare different modes of communicating a design (sketch vs verbal description vs labelled diagram) — discuss which modes are clearest for different audiences
success_criteria: Another student can describe back what the design proposes
Includes at least one feature that addresses the user's need

nodes.label: Comparing designs against user stories and criteria
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare at least two design ideas against user stories and design criteria and give reasons for preferring one
nodes.minimum_width: Given two design ideas and a user story, state which idea better meets the user's need and give one reason linked to the user story or a criterion
nodes.typical_width: Compare multiple design ideas against user stories and criteria for a range of problem contexts; identify which ideas meet the criteria and which miss aspects of the user's need; provide reasons for judgements
wider: Compare designs for a problem where different users have different needs — for example, a recycling encouragement tool used by different age groups — discuss how a design that suits one user story might not suit another
Explore what happens when no design idea fully meets all criteria — discuss how to decide between imperfect options and whether criteria can be prioritised

response_modes.reason: Comparing against criteria requires students to make a judgement move — not just describe the designs but evaluate them against a standard. The reasoning scaffold (does this design meet criterion X? does that one?) prevents students from selecting on preference alone.

This node integrates the design ideas generated in node 1 with the user stories and criteria from AC9TDI4P01. The comparison task only works when students bring both design ideas and problem definition together — coordination across the design process is the learning.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The wider tier — competing user stories, imperfect criteria trade-offs — introduces design judgement that is rich beyond the minimum. These are genuine decision-making contexts that advance students' understanding of why design comparison matters, not just how to do it procedurally.
success_criteria: Names at least one criterion or user story element when comparing designs
States a preference and connects it to a reason beyond personal taste
